title: Public libraries study
text: You have agreed to take part in a research study about how people use public libraries. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Thanks for joining us. To start, can you tell me about the last time you visited a library and what you did there?
explanation: Sure. The last time I went to a library was about two weeks ago, and I mainly went there to study. My apartment is pretty noisy because I share it with two roommates, so I needed a quiet place to prepare for an exam. I found a desk by the window on the second floor and stayed for almost four hours. Before I left, I also borrowed a novel, just something light to read on the bus. Honestly, I'd say I go there more for the quiet atmosphere than for the books themselves, but it's nice to have both in one place.
points: Answers the question in the first sentence with a specific visit
Explains the reason for the visit
Adds concrete details such as time, place or activity
Uses past tenses accurately and sounds natural

stem: Some people prefer to study in a library, while others prefer to study at home. Which do you prefer, and why?
explanation: I definitely prefer studying in a library. The main reason is that I focus much better when I'm away from home. At home there are too many distractions, like my bed, the TV and my phone, and I end up taking breaks every ten minutes. In a library, everyone around me is working too, so I feel a kind of positive pressure to keep going. For example, last semester I wrote most of my history paper at the library in just three afternoons, and I'm sure it would've taken me a week at home. So for serious work, the library wins for me.
points: Gives a main reason linked to concentration or resources
Supports the reason with a personal example

stem: Many cities are reducing library budgets because so much information is now available online. Do you think public libraries are still important? Why or why not?
explanation: Yes, I think public libraries are still really important, maybe even more than before. First of all, not everyone has a fast internet connection or a computer at home, and the library gives those people free access. Second, libraries do a lot more than lend books. In my town, for instance, the library runs homework clubs for kids and free computer classes for older people. Those services help people who might otherwise be left behind. Also, online information isn't always reliable, and librarians can help you find trustworthy sources. So I'd say cutting library budgets is a mistake.
points: Takes a clear position in the first sentence
Gives at least two reasons, such as access and community services
Includes a specific example from experience

stem: Finally, how do you think public libraries will change in the next twenty years?
explanation: I think libraries will become more like community centers than places to store books. We'll probably see fewer printed books on the shelves, because more people will read e-books and use online databases. But I don't think the buildings will disappear. Instead, I'd expect more space for group study rooms, technology labs and events. For example, my local library recently added a room with 3D printers and recording equipment, and it's always busy with young people. So I believe the library of the future will be less about borrowing and more about learning, creating and meeting other people.
points: Makes a clear prediction at the start
Explains why the change is likely
Gives an example of a current trend that supports the prediction
Uses future forms such as 'will' and 'probably' naturally

title: Getting around the city
text: You are taking part in a study about how people travel around their city every day. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Let's begin. How do you usually get to school or work, and how long does the trip take?
explanation: Usually I take the bus, and the trip takes about thirty-five minutes each way. There's a stop right outside my building, so it's really convenient. The bus goes straight down the main road and drops me off just two blocks from campus. I normally use the time to listen to podcasts or review my notes before class. On days when it's sunny and I'm not in a hurry, I sometimes ride my bike instead, which is actually a little faster, around twenty-five minutes. But in winter or when it rains, the bus is definitely my first choice.
points: Names the usual way of traveling in the first sentence
Gives the length of the trip and other details
Mentions how the time is used or an alternative

stem: If you could choose, would you rather travel by public transportation or by car? Why?
explanation: I'd rather use public transportation, even though a car might seem more comfortable. The biggest reason is stress. When I drive, I have to deal with traffic and look for parking, and that can be really frustrating in the city center. On a train or a bus, I can just sit back, read something or answer messages. It's also a lot cheaper. For example, my cousin drives to work every day, and between gas and parking he spends almost three times what I pay for my monthly pass. So for everyday trips, public transportation makes more sense to me.
points: Gives a clear choice at once
Explains the main reason, such as stress or cost
Adds a comparison or a concrete example
Uses 'I'd rather' or similar natural phrases

stem: Some people say cities should ban cars from their downtown areas. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I mostly agree, but I think it should be done carefully. On the positive side, a downtown without cars would be quieter, safer and much cleaner. People could walk and cycle without worrying about traffic, and cafés and shops could use the extra space. I visited a city last year where the old center was car-free, and it felt so relaxed and friendly. However, cities would need to provide good buses and parking at the edge of the area, because older people and delivery drivers still need access. So yes, I support the idea, as long as there are real alternatives.
points: States a position in the first sentence, even a qualified one
Uses a personal example to support the view

stem: How do you think the way people travel in cities will change in the future?
explanation: I think we'll see a lot more shared and electric transportation. Already, in many cities you can rent electric scooters or bikes with your phone, and I expect that to grow because it's cheap and convenient for short trips. I also think fewer young people will want to own a car. My friends, for example, mostly use ride-sharing apps or public transportation, and none of them are in a hurry to buy a car. In the long run, self-driving buses might become common too. So overall, I'd say city travel will become more flexible and probably cleaner.
points: Explains why the trend is likely
Supports the prediction with something already happening

title: Online learning research
text: You have agreed to take part in a university study about online learning. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: First, have you ever taken an online class or course? Tell me about your experience.
explanation: Yes, I took an online course in basic statistics last summer, and overall it was a good experience. The course had short video lectures, weekly quizzes and a discussion board where we could ask questions. What I liked most was that I could watch the videos whenever I wanted, so I was able to keep my part-time job at the same time. The hardest part was staying motivated, because nobody was checking on me in person. A few weeks I fell behind and had to catch up on the weekend. But I finished it and got a good grade.
points: Answers yes or no with a specific course
Mentions one positive and one difficulty

stem: Do you prefer learning online or in a traditional classroom? Why?
explanation: I prefer a traditional classroom, mainly because of the interaction. When I'm in a room with a teacher and classmates, I can ask questions right away and hear other people's ideas. That really helps me understand difficult topics. Online, I sometimes feel like I'm just watching videos alone. For example, in my chemistry class this year, a lot of my understanding came from quick conversations with my lab partner, and that just doesn't happen the same way on a screen. That said, online learning is great for flexibility, so I'd say a mix of both would be ideal for me.
points: States a preference in the first sentence
Gives a reason based on interaction or flexibility
Supports it with a specific example

stem: Some educators believe online courses can be just as effective as in-person courses. What is your opinion?
explanation: I think online courses can be just as effective, but only for certain subjects and certain students. For subjects that are mostly about information, like history or business theory, a well-designed online course works really well. Students can pause, rewatch and study at their own speed. But for subjects with hands-on practice, like nursing or lab science, being in person is hard to replace. It also depends on the learner. My younger brother, for instance, struggled with online school because he needed a fixed schedule. So I'd say online courses are effective when the subject and the student are a good match.
points: Gives a clear opinion, even a qualified one
Explains when online learning works and when it does not
Concludes by restating the main point

stem: Finally, do you think universities will offer more online programs in the future? What effect might this have?
explanation: Yes, I'm pretty sure universities will offer more online programs. Technology keeps improving, and many students want to study while working or living far from campus. One big effect will be that education becomes more accessible. Someone in a small town, for example, could earn a degree from a university in another country without moving. On the other hand, campuses might feel emptier, and students could miss out on the social side of university, like clubs and friendships. So I think online programs will open doors for a lot of people, but universities will need to find ways to keep students connected.
points: Uses an example to make the effect concrete

title: Exercise and health habits
text: You are participating in a study about people's exercise habits. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: To start, what kind of exercise do you do in a typical week?
explanation: In a typical week I go running two or three times and play soccer with friends on Saturday. I usually run early in the morning, before classes, for about thirty minutes in the park near my home. It wakes me up and helps me feel more focused for the rest of the day. The soccer game on Saturday is more about having fun, though. A group of us from my dormitory meet at the university field, and we play for about two hours. During exam weeks I don't always manage to run, but I try to keep the Saturday game no matter what.
points: Names the types of exercise directly
Explains why the activity is done
Uses present simple and frequency adverbs well

stem: Would you rather exercise alone or with other people? Why?
explanation: I'd rather exercise with other people, at least most of the time. When I'm with friends, exercise feels less like a duty and more like a social activity, so I'm much more likely to actually do it. Other people also push me to work harder. For example, when I joined a running group last spring, I started running longer distances, just because I didn't want to fall behind the others. When I run alone, I often stop early. That said, I do enjoy a quiet run by myself now and then, especially when I need to clear my head.
points: States a clear preference at the start
Gives a reason such as motivation
Supports it with a personal example

stem: Some people think schools should require students to do physical exercise every day. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: Yes, I agree that schools should include some physical activity every day. First, a lot of young people spend hours sitting, both in class and in front of screens at home, so school might be their only chance to move. Second, exercise actually helps learning. I remember that at my high school, we had a short sports period in the morning, and I always felt more awake in the classes afterward. It doesn't have to be intense or competitive, though. Even a twenty-minute walk or some simple games would be enough to make a difference.
points: Takes a clear position in the first sentence
Gives two reasons, health and learning
Supports a reason with personal experience
Suggests a realistic way to do it

stem: How do you think technology will affect the way people exercise in the future?
explanation: I think technology will make exercise more personal and maybe more fun. Already, lots of people use fitness watches that count their steps and track their heart rate, and those devices will probably get smarter and give advice like a personal trainer. I also expect more people to exercise at home with online classes or virtual reality games. My sister, for example, does a cycling class at home where she races against people in other countries, and she loves it. The risk is that people might rely on gadgets too much, but overall I think technology will encourage more people to stay active.

title: Food and cooking habits
text: You have agreed to take part in a research project about cooking and eating habits. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Let's start with your own habits. How often do you cook for yourself, and what do you usually make?
explanation: I cook for myself about four or five times a week, usually in the evening. I'm not an expert, so I keep it simple. Most of the time I make rice with vegetables and some chicken or lentils, which is cheap, healthy and fast. On weekends I like to try something a bit more interesting, like a pasta dish or a curry from a recipe my mother sent me. I usually cook a big amount on Sunday and keep some in the fridge for lunch on Monday and Tuesday. That way I save both time and money during the busy part of the week.
points: Answers how often in the first sentence
Explains a reason or habit, such as saving time

stem: Do you prefer eating at home or eating at restaurants? Why?
explanation: I prefer eating at home most of the time. The main reason is that I know exactly what's in my food. Restaurant meals often have a lot of salt, oil and sugar, and the portions are huge, so I usually feel heavy afterward. At home I can make something lighter and healthier. It's also much cheaper. For example, a meal for two at the café near my campus costs about the same as all my groceries for three days. Of course, I still enjoy going out with friends for a birthday or a celebration, but for everyday meals, home is better.
points: States a preference clearly at the start
Gives reasons such as health and cost
Includes a specific comparison or example
Mentions when the other option is good

stem: Some people believe cooking should be taught as a required subject in high schools. What do you think?
explanation: I think that's a great idea. Cooking is a basic life skill, but many young people leave home without knowing how to make a simple meal. As a result, they end up spending a lot on fast food, which isn't good for their health or their budget. When I moved into my first apartment, for instance, I lived on instant noodles for a month because I didn't know how to cook anything else. A cooking class could also teach useful things like nutrition, food safety and planning a budget. So yes, I'd make it part of the high school program.
points: Explains why cooking is a useful skill
Supports the view with a personal example
Mentions what such a class could include

stem: In the future, do you think people will cook more or less at home? Why?
explanation: I think people will probably cook less at home in the future. Food delivery apps are getting faster and cheaper, and many people are working longer hours, so ordering a meal is just easier. In my building, for example, I see delivery drivers arriving almost every evening. Also, supermarkets now sell lots of ready-made meals that only need a few minutes in the microwave. On the other hand, there's a growing interest in healthy eating, and some people enjoy cooking as a hobby. But overall, I'd say convenience will win for most people, so home cooking will decrease.
points: Gives reasons connected to current trends

title: Music in everyday life
text: You are taking part in a study about the role of music in people's lives. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Tell me a little about when and where you usually listen to music.
explanation: I listen to music pretty much every day, mostly when I'm commuting or doing chores. On the bus in the morning I put on my headphones and listen to upbeat songs to wake myself up. In the evening, when I'm cooking or cleaning my room, I usually play something more relaxing through a small speaker. The only time I don't listen to music is when I'm studying, because song lyrics distract me. If I really need background sound, I choose instrumental music, like piano or soft jazz. So music is a big part of my routine, but I'm careful about when I use it.
points: Gives specific situations and types of music
Explains a reason for the habit

stem: Do you prefer listening to recorded music or going to live concerts? Why?
explanation: Honestly, I prefer live concerts, even though I don't go very often. There's an energy at a live show that you just can't get from headphones. You're surrounded by people who love the same music, and the musicians react to the crowd, so every performance is a little different. Last year, for example, I saw a local band at an outdoor festival, and when everyone started singing together, it was one of the best nights I've had. Recorded music is more convenient and much cheaper, of course, so I listen to it more. But if I had to choose, I'd pick live music.
points: Gives a reason about atmosphere or experience
Supports it with a specific memory
Acknowledges the advantage of the other option

stem: Some people think every child should learn to play a musical instrument. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I agree that every child should at least have the chance to learn an instrument. Learning music teaches patience and discipline, because you have to practice regularly to improve. It can also help with other subjects, like math and memory. I learned the guitar when I was ten, and the habit of practicing a little every day really helped me later with studying. However, I don't think it should be forced. If a child really hates it, it can become a source of stress. So I'd say schools should offer music lessons to everyone, but children should be able to choose.
points: Gives a clear position at the start
Uses a personal example as support
Adds a reasonable condition or limit

stem: How do you think technology will change the way people create or listen to music in the future?
explanation: I think technology will make it much easier for ordinary people to create music. Even now, you can make a song on your phone with free apps, without knowing how to play any instrument. My roommate, for example, records short tracks in our apartment and shares them online, and some of them have thousands of plays. In the future, I expect artificial intelligence tools to help people write melodies and mix songs in minutes. For listeners, music will probably be even more personal, with apps choosing songs based on your mood. The challenge will be for professional musicians to stand out.
points: Mentions an effect on musicians or listeners

title: Travel and tourism
text: You have agreed to take part in a survey about travel and tourism. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: To begin, can you describe a trip you've taken that you really enjoyed?
explanation: Sure. One trip I really enjoyed was a week in the mountains in the north of my country, about two years ago. I went with three friends from school, and we stayed in a small guesthouse in a village. Every day we hiked to a different lake or viewpoint, and in the evenings the owner cooked us traditional food. What made it special was how peaceful it was. There was hardly any phone signal, so we actually talked to each other and played cards instead of checking our screens. I came back feeling completely relaxed, and I'd love to go back someday.
points: Gives details of where, when and who

stem: When you travel, do you prefer to follow a detailed plan or to be spontaneous? Why?
explanation: I prefer to have a basic plan but leave room to be spontaneous. I like to book my transportation and where I'm staying before I go, because that saves stress and usually money. But I don't plan every hour of the day. Some of my best travel memories happened by chance. For example, on a trip to a coastal town, a shop owner told us about a fishing festival in the next village, so we changed our plans and went. It turned out to be the highlight of the trip. So a little planning is good, but too much takes the fun away.
points: Gives a clear answer at the start
Explains the reasoning for each part
Supports the view with a specific travel example

stem: Some people say tourism does more harm than good to popular destinations. What is your opinion?
explanation: I don't think tourism does more harm than good, but it can definitely cause problems if it isn't managed well. On the positive side, tourism creates jobs and brings money to local businesses, like hotels, restaurants and guides. In many small towns, it's the main source of income. But when too many visitors arrive at once, it can damage nature and make prices go up for local people. I've seen beaches covered in litter after a busy holiday weekend, for example. So I'd say the answer is to control visitor numbers and educate tourists, not to stop tourism.
points: Discusses benefits and harms as reasons
Suggests a solution in the conclusion

stem: How do you think people's travel habits will change over the next few decades?
explanation: I think people will travel differently, with more focus on the environment and on longer, slower trips. Many travelers are already worried about the pollution caused by flying, so I expect more people to choose trains for shorter distances. Also, since more people can work remotely now, I think they'll stay in one place for weeks or even months instead of rushing through five cities in a week. A friend of mine, for instance, worked from a small seaside town for two months last year. Technology like virtual tours might also let people explore places before they decide to go.
points: Gives reasons tied to current trends

title: Volunteering study
text: You are participating in a research study about volunteering and community work. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Have you ever done any volunteer work? Please tell me about it.
explanation: Yes, I volunteered at an animal shelter for about six months when I was in high school. I went every Saturday morning, and my main jobs were cleaning the cages, feeding the dogs and taking them for walks. Sometimes I also helped families who came in to adopt a pet by showing them around. It was hard work, and it was a little sad to see so many animals without homes. But it felt great when a dog I'd been caring for finally found a family. That experience made me much more responsible, and I still visit the shelter sometimes.
points: Answers yes or no with a specific example
Describes the tasks and how often

stem: Would you rather volunteer for a local organization or for an international one? Why?
explanation: I'd rather volunteer for a local organization. The main reason is that I can see the results of my work directly. If I help at a community center in my neighborhood, I meet the people I'm helping, and I can keep going every week. With an international organization, I'd probably have to travel far or only help online, and it's harder to feel connected. For example, my friend helps teach reading to children at a library near our university, and she can actually see their progress over the year. That kind of steady, personal contact seems more meaningful to me.
points: States a preference in the first sentence
Gives a reason related to impact or connection

stem: Some schools require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours before they graduate. Do you think this is a good idea?
explanation: I think it's a good idea overall. A lot of students would never try volunteering unless they had to, and once they do it, many of them discover they actually enjoy it. It also teaches skills that you don't learn in class, like teamwork, communication and responsibility. At my school we needed forty hours, and I chose a food bank because a friend was going. I ended up staying long after I'd finished my hours. One concern is that some students just do it for the certificate. But even then, I think they learn something about their community.
points: Gives a clear opinion at the start

stem: Do you think people in the future will volunteer more or less than people do today? Why?
explanation: I think people will probably volunteer more, but in different ways. Technology is making it easier to find volunteer opportunities that fit your schedule. There are already apps where you can sign up for a two-hour job, like helping at a park cleanup, without making a long commitment. I've used one myself a couple of times. Online volunteering will grow too, for example tutoring students or translating documents from home. On the other hand, people are very busy, so long-term volunteering might decrease. But overall, I think short, flexible volunteering will become more popular, so the total amount will grow.
points: Includes a personal or concrete example

title: Smartphones and daily life
text: You have agreed to take part in a study about how smartphones affect daily life. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: First, can you describe how you use your smartphone on a normal day?
explanation: I use my phone all day, from the moment I wake up. My alarm is on my phone, and the first thing I do is check messages and the weather. During the day, I mainly use it for university things, like reading emails from professors, checking my class schedule and looking up words I don't know. I also use a map app because I'm still learning my way around the city. In the evening, I relax by watching short videos or chatting with my family back home. Honestly, I'd guess I spend around four hours a day on it in total.
points: Answers directly with a clear overview
Describes uses at different times of the day
Ends with a natural personal comment

stem: When you want to contact a friend, do you prefer to send a text message or make a phone call? Why?
explanation: I usually prefer sending a text message. The main reason is that it's less demanding for both people. My friends and I all have busy schedules, and a text lets them answer when they're free instead of interrupting a class or work. It also gives me time to think about what I want to say. For example, when I invite friends to dinner, I just send a group message, and everyone replies within an hour. That said, if something important or emotional happens, I always call, because hearing someone's voice feels much more personal.
points: Gives a reason such as convenience
Supports it with an everyday example
Notes when the other option is better

stem: Some people believe children under twelve should not have their own smartphones. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I mostly agree. Children under twelve aren't usually ready to manage the amount of content and contact a smartphone gives them. They can easily spend hours on games or videos instead of playing outside, reading or sleeping. There are also safety risks, like talking to strangers online. My cousin got a phone at nine, and her parents told me her grades dropped because she was always on it. That said, a simple phone just for calls and messages could be useful for safety, for example when a child walks home alone. So I'd say a basic phone is fine, but not a smartphone.
points: Takes a clear position in the first sentence
Gives reasons about time use and safety
Supports the view with an example

stem: How do you think smartphones, or the devices that replace them, will change in the next ten to fifteen years?
explanation: I think phones will become less like something we hold and more like something we wear. We already have smart watches and earbuds that can answer calls and give directions, so maybe in ten years we'll use smart glasses that show information right in front of our eyes. I also expect voice control to become much more common, so we'll type less. My grandfather, for example, already prefers talking to his phone instead of typing, and that's only going to grow. The big question will be privacy, because these devices will know even more about us than phones do now.
points: Links the prediction to existing devices
Raises a broader issue, such as privacy

title: Reading habits
text: You are taking part in a research study about people's reading habits. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Let's start. What kinds of things do you read in a typical week, apart from schoolwork?
explanation: Apart from schoolwork, I mostly read news articles and novels. Every morning I spend about fifteen minutes reading the news on my phone while I have breakfast, mainly about science and sports. In the evenings, I try to read a few chapters of a novel before bed, usually a mystery or science fiction story. Right now I'm reading a detective novel that a friend recommended, and it's really hard to put down. I also read a lot of online reviews, for example before I buy something or choose a restaurant. So I'd say I read every day, just in different forms.
points: Gives details about when and how much

stem: Do you prefer reading printed books or e-books? Why?
explanation: I prefer printed books, especially for longer reading. I find it easier to concentrate on paper, because there are no notifications popping up, and my eyes don't get as tired as they do with a screen. I also like being able to see how far I've read and flip back to an earlier page quickly. For example, when I read a long novel last month, I kept a pencil inside to mark parts I liked, and I just enjoyed holding the book. E-books are useful when I travel, since I can carry many at once, but at home I always choose paper.
points: Explains reasons such as focus or comfort
Mentions when the other option is useful

stem: Some people say that young people today read less than earlier generations did. Do you think this is true? Why or why not?
explanation: I think it's partly true, but it depends on what you count as reading. Young people probably read fewer printed books than their grandparents did, because there are so many other kinds of entertainment, like streaming and video games. But at the same time, they read a huge amount online: messages, articles, forum posts and even fan fiction. My younger sister, for example, rarely reads books, but she reads long online stories every night. The difference is that a lot of this reading is short and fast. So I'd say young people read just as much, but less deeply.
points: Supports the point with an example

stem: Do you think printed books will still be common fifty years from now?
explanation: Yes, I think printed books will still be around, although they'll probably be less common than now. Many people said that e-books would replace paper books completely, but that hasn't happened. In fact, in my city a few new independent bookstores have opened recently, and they're always busy. I think people like printed books as objects. They make good gifts, and they're nice to collect. However, for things like textbooks, manuals and news, I expect digital versions to take over almost completely because they're cheaper and easier to update. So paper books will survive mostly for pleasure reading.
points: Supports it with evidence from current trends

title: Teamwork and group projects
text: You have agreed to take part in a study about how students work in teams. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Can you tell me about a group project you worked on recently?
explanation: Sure. Last semester I worked on a group project for my marketing class. There were four of us, and we had to create a plan to promote a new local café. We split the work so that each person had a part: one did research on customers, one designed the social media posts, and I prepared the budget. We met every Thursday in the library to put everything together. The final presentation went really well, and the café owner even used some of our ideas. The hardest part was finding times when everyone was free, but we managed it.
points: Identifies a specific project at once
Explains the task and how work was divided
Mentions the result and a difficulty

stem: Do you prefer working on assignments alone or as part of a group? Why?
explanation: I generally prefer working alone, at least for written assignments. When I work by myself, I can choose my own schedule and work at my own speed, and I don't have to wait for others or worry that someone isn't doing their part. For example, in one group essay I did last year, two members sent their sections the night before the deadline, and I had to rewrite a lot of it. That was really stressful. However, I do think groups are better for big projects that need different skills, like designing a product. So it depends on the task.
points: Gives reasons such as control and reliability
Recognizes when the other option works better

stem: Some professors think group projects are the best way to prepare students for the workplace. Do you agree?
explanation: Yes, I largely agree. In most jobs, people rarely work completely alone. They have to share tasks, communicate with colleagues and solve problems together, and group projects are good practice for that. You learn how to deal with different personalities and how to compromise. During my internship last summer, for instance, I was put on a team with people from three departments, and my experience with class projects really helped me feel comfortable speaking up in meetings. The only problem is that grading can be unfair. So professors should also check how much each student actually contributed.
points: Explains how group work matches real jobs
Gives a concrete example such as an internship
Mentions a weakness and a fix

stem: In the future, do you think more teamwork will happen online rather than face to face? What might the effects be?
explanation: I think so, yes. Many companies already have teams spread across different cities or even countries, and tools like video calls and shared documents make that easy. The good side is that people can work with the best person for a job, wherever they live. My aunt, for example, works with designers in four countries without ever meeting them. But online teamwork has some downsides. It's harder to build trust and friendship through a screen, and small misunderstandings can grow because you can't read people's body language. So I think teams will need to meet in person sometimes too.
points: Supports the answer with an example

title: Sleep and study habits
text: You are participating in a university study about students' sleep and study habits. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: To begin, could you describe your usual sleep schedule during the school week?
explanation: During the school week I usually go to bed around midnight and wake up at about seven, so I get roughly seven hours of sleep. My first class starts at eight thirty, and I like to have time for breakfast and to review my notes. To be honest, my schedule isn't always regular. When I have an exam or a big assignment due, I sometimes stay up until two, and then I'm really tired the next day. On weekends I sleep much later, often until ten, to catch up. I know that's not ideal, but it's pretty common among my friends.

stem: Do you study better in the morning or late at night? Why?
explanation: I definitely study better in the morning. After a night's sleep, my mind feels fresh, and I can concentrate on difficult material like math problems much more easily. Also, it's quieter, because most of my roommates are still asleep and nobody is messaging me yet. At night, on the other hand, I'm usually tired after a full day of classes, and I end up reading the same page three times. For example, before my last chemistry exam, I studied from six to eight every morning for a week, and I got one of my best grades. So mornings work best for me.
points: Gives reasons such as energy and quiet
Supports it with a specific example

stem: Some universities are considering starting morning classes later so that students can sleep more. Do you think this is a good idea?
explanation: I think it's a good idea. Many students don't get enough sleep, partly because of part-time jobs and long study hours, and an early class makes it even worse. When students are tired, they don't pay attention and they don't remember much, so the class is less useful. In my own experience, I've almost fallen asleep in eight a.m. lectures, even when the topic was interesting. Starting at nine or nine thirty could make a real difference. Some people might say students would just stay up later, but I think most would use the extra time to rest.
points: Takes a clear position at the start
Gives reasons linked to learning and health

stem: Do you think people in general will get more sleep or less sleep in the future? Why?
explanation: I'm afraid people will probably get less sleep in the future. More and more people use screens late at night, whether they're working, watching shows or scrolling through social media, and that makes it harder to fall asleep. Also, with online work, many people feel they need to be available at all hours. My father, for instance, often answers work emails at eleven at night. On the positive side, people are becoming more aware of how important sleep is, and there are apps that remind you to go to bed. But I think the pressure of technology will be stronger.
points: Explains reasons tied to technology and work

title: Shopping habits
text: You have agreed to take part in a market research study about shopping habits. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Tell me about the last thing you bought and how you bought it.
explanation: The last thing I bought was a pair of running shoes, about a week ago. I actually bought them in a sports store near my apartment, even though I usually shop online. My old shoes had become uncomfortable, and I wanted to try different sizes before choosing, because every brand fits a little differently. The salesperson let me test a few pairs on a small running machine in the store, which was really helpful. They cost a bit more than online, about ten dollars more, but I was happy to pay that to be sure they fit well.
points: Names the item and when it was bought
Explains how and where it was bought
Gives a reason for that choice

stem: In general, do you prefer shopping online or in physical stores? Why?
explanation: In general, I prefer shopping online. The main reason is convenience. I can compare prices from different shops in a few minutes, read reviews from other buyers and order things at any time, even late at night. As a student, I don't have much free time, so I don't want to spend a whole afternoon going from store to store. For example, I bought most of my textbooks online this year and saved about thirty percent compared to the campus bookstore. However, for clothes and shoes, I still like going to a store, because I want to try things on first.
points: Explains reasons like convenience and price
Supports it with a specific example

stem: Some people worry that online shopping is causing small local shops to close. Do you think governments should do something to protect local shops?
explanation: Yes, I think governments should help local shops to some degree. Small shops are important for neighborhoods. They create local jobs, and they make streets feel lively and safe. When they close, the area can become empty and less pleasant. In my hometown, for example, three shops on the main street closed in one year, and now that part of town feels quite lonely. Governments could lower taxes for small businesses or help them set up their own online stores. I don't think they should punish online companies, though. The goal should be to help local shops compete.

stem: How do you think shopping will be different twenty years from now?
explanation: I think shopping will be much more automatic and personal in twenty years. Apps will probably know what we need before we do. For instance, your fridge might notice that you're out of milk and order it for you. I also expect deliveries to be extremely fast, maybe within an hour, possibly by drones in some places. Physical stores won't disappear, but I think they'll become more like showrooms where you go to see and try products, and then they're delivered to your home. Some supermarkets near me already have no cashiers, so that change has already started.
points: Makes a clear prediction at the start
Gives specific examples of future changes
Links the prediction to a current trend

title: Museums and cultural visits
text: You are taking part in a study about how people use museums and cultural sites. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: When was the last time you visited a museum, and what did you see there?
explanation: The last time I visited a museum was about three months ago, when my parents came to visit me. We went to the natural history museum downtown and spent most of the afternoon there. The best part was the hall with the dinosaur skeletons. Some of them were enormous, and there were screens that showed how scientists think the animals moved. We also saw an exhibition about ocean life, with a huge model of a whale hanging from the ceiling. My parents loved it, and I realized I should go to museums more often, since there are so many in this city.
points: Answers when in the first sentence
Describes what was seen with details

stem: Do you prefer visiting art museums or science museums? Why?
explanation: I prefer science museums. I enjoy places where I can learn how things work, and science museums usually have lots of interactive exhibits, so you're not just looking at things behind glass. You can press buttons, try experiments and see the results right away. For example, at one science museum I visited, there was a room where you could create small earthquakes and see how different buildings react. I still remember it years later. Art museums can be beautiful, but sometimes I don't understand the meaning of the works without a guide, so I enjoy them less.
points: Gives a reason linked to learning or interaction
Briefly compares with the other type

stem: Some people think museums should be free for everyone. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I agree that museums should be free, or at least free for students and families with low incomes. Museums hold a country's history, art and science, and I think everyone should have the chance to learn from them, not only people who can afford a ticket. When museums are free, more people visit, including people who would never think of going otherwise. In my city, for example, the history museum is free on Sundays, and it's always full of families with children. Of course, museums need money, so governments or donors would have to support them.
points: Supports it with a local example

stem: Do you think virtual museum tours will one day replace real visits? Why or why not?
explanation: No, I don't think virtual tours will replace real visits, although they'll become more popular. Virtual tours are great for people who live far away or who want to prepare before a trip. I've used one to look around a famous gallery in another country, and it was impressive. But it didn't feel the same as being there. Standing in front of a huge painting or a real dinosaur skeleton gives you a sense of size and detail that a screen can't. Visiting a museum is also a social experience, something you share with friends or family. So both will exist together.
points: Explains the benefits of virtual tours
Explains why real visits are still valuable

title: Saving energy at home
text: You have agreed to take part in a research project about energy use at home. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: First, what do you or your family do at home to save energy?
explanation: We try to do a few simple things at home to save energy. First, we always turn off the lights when we leave a room, and a couple of years ago we replaced all the old bulbs with LED ones, which use much less electricity. We also unplug things like the TV and phone chargers at night. In summer, instead of using the air conditioner all day, we close the curtains in the afternoon to keep the heat out and use fans. My mother is very strict about it, partly to protect the environment, but mostly because it lowers our bills.
points: Answers directly with a clear overview

stem: If you were choosing a home, would you rather live in a large house in the suburbs or a small apartment in the city? Why?
explanation: I'd rather live in a small apartment in the city. The main reason is convenience. In the city, I could walk or take the train to school, work and shops, so I wouldn't need a car. That saves both time and money. A small apartment is also easier and cheaper to heat and clean. For example, my friend moved from a big house to a small apartment downtown last year, and she said her energy bills went down by almost half. A big house with a garden sounds nice, but I don't think I'd use all that space.
points: Explains reasons such as convenience and cost

stem: Some people think governments should require all new homes to have solar panels. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I mostly agree with that idea. Solar panels reduce pollution because homes produce some of their own clean electricity, and over time they also save families money on their bills. If it's required only for new homes, builders can plan for it from the start, which is cheaper than adding panels later. In my neighborhood, a few new houses already have them, and the owners say their summer bills are almost zero. However, solar panels don't work well everywhere, for example in very shady areas. So I'd support the rule, but with some exceptions where it doesn't make sense.

stem: How do you think the way homes use energy will change in the future?
explanation: I think homes will become much smarter about energy. Already, some people have thermostats that learn their daily routine and lower the heating when no one's home. In the future, I expect most appliances to work like that, running the washing machine, for example, at times when electricity is cheapest. I also think more homes will store their own energy in batteries, maybe even using their electric car as a battery. My uncle has solar panels and a home battery, and he hardly buys any electricity now. So I'd say homes will use less energy and produce more of their own.
points: Supports the prediction with a real example

title: Part-time jobs for students
text: You are participating in a study about students who work while they study. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Have you ever had a part-time job while studying? Tell me about it.
explanation: Yes, I worked part-time at a bakery during my last two years of high school. I worked there on Saturday and Sunday mornings, from six until noon. My job was to serve customers, put fresh bread on the shelves and clean the counters at the end of my shift. Getting up so early was hard at first, but I got used to it. I really liked the owner, an older man who taught me how to talk politely to difficult customers. I saved most of my pay, and that money helped me buy my first laptop for university.
points: Answers yes or no with a specific job
Mentions what was learned or gained

stem: Would you rather have a job related to your studies or any job that pays well? Why?
explanation: I'd rather have a job related to my studies, even if it pays a little less. The experience would help me much more in the long run. For example, I'm studying computer science, so working at a campus IT office would teach me real skills and give me something useful to put on my resume. A friend of mine worked as a teaching assistant in the biology department, and that job helped her get a research position after graduation. Good pay is important, of course, especially for rent, but I think useful experience is worth more than a few extra dollars an hour.

stem: Some people believe that working while studying harms students' grades. Others think it teaches valuable skills. What is your view?
explanation: I think working while studying is mostly positive, as long as the hours are reasonable. A part-time job teaches skills you can't learn in class, like managing your time, dealing with customers and being responsible. It also helps students understand the value of money. When I worked at the bakery, I actually became more organized with my homework, because I had less free time and couldn't waste it. But if a student works more than about fifteen or twenty hours a week, I think their grades will probably suffer. So the key is balance, not avoiding work completely.

stem: Do you think it will become more common or less common for students to work during their studies in the future? Why?
explanation: I think it will become more common. The cost of university and housing keeps going up in many places, so more students will need to earn money while they study. At the same time, it's becoming easier to find flexible work. Many students now do jobs like online tutoring, graphic design or delivery, where they can choose their own hours. One of my classmates, for example, edits videos for small businesses from his dorm room. Employers also seem to value work experience more and more, so students will see a job as a way to prepare for their future career.
points: Mentions the link to future careers

title: How people get the news
text: You have agreed to take part in a study about how people find out about news and current events. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: To start, how do you usually find out what is happening in the world?
explanation: Mostly I find out about the news through my phone. In the morning I check a couple of news apps while I'm having coffee, and I read the headlines and maybe two or three full articles. During the day I also see news on social media, but I'm a bit careful with that, because not everything there is accurate. Once a week or so, I listen to a news podcast that explains one big story in more detail, usually while I'm walking to class. I almost never watch the news on TV, though. My parents do, but I don't.
points: Answers the question in the first sentence
Gives details about when and how

stem: Do you prefer reading the news or watching news videos? Why?
explanation: I prefer reading the news. When I read, I can go at my own speed, skip the parts I already know and spend more time on the details that interest me. It's also easier to check the facts, because I can look at the sources or open another article right away. Videos are often quite short, and they focus on dramatic pictures more than explanations. For example, when there was a big economic story recently, a two-minute video didn't really help me understand it, but a longer article explained it clearly. That said, videos can be useful for events like sports or weather.
points: Explains reasons such as speed and depth
Notes when the other option works

stem: Many people now get their news from social media. Do you think this is a positive or negative development? Why?
explanation: I think it's mostly negative, although there are some benefits. On the positive side, news spreads very quickly on social media, and you can hear from ordinary people who are actually at an event. But the big problem is that false information spreads just as fast, and many people share stories without checking them. Also, social media shows you mostly what you already agree with, so people don't see other points of view. My uncle, for example, believed a fake health story he saw online and shared it with the whole family. So I think people need to learn to check their sources.
points: Gives a benefit and a stronger drawback
Supports the view with an example

stem: How do you think the way people get news will change in the future?
explanation: I think news will become even more personal and more audio-based. Already, apps choose stories based on what you've read before, and I expect that to grow, so two people might see completely different news in the morning. I also think more people will listen to the news through smart speakers or earbuds, because they can do it while cooking or driving. My roommate, for instance, gets a short news summary from her speaker every morning while she gets ready. The risk is that people will only hear what they want, so trusted news organizations will be more important than ever.
points: Explains the reasons for the change
Raises a broader issue at the end

title: Learning languages
text: You are taking part in a research study about learning foreign languages. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Can you tell me about your experience learning English or another language?
explanation: I started learning English at school when I was about eight, but for a long time I only studied grammar and vocabulary lists, and I couldn't really speak. Things changed when I was fifteen and started watching TV series in English with subtitles. Little by little, I began to understand natural conversation, and I learned a lot of everyday expressions that weren't in my textbooks. Later, I joined an online group where I practiced speaking with people from other countries once a week. That was scary at first, but it improved my confidence a lot. Now I'm preparing for university study abroad.
points: Answers directly with when learning began
Uses past tenses and time expressions well

stem: Do you think it's better to learn a language in a classroom or by living in a country where it's spoken? Why?
explanation: I think living in the country is better, although classes are useful at the beginning. When you live in a place where the language is spoken, you have to use it every day, at the store, on the bus and with neighbors, so you learn much faster. You also learn how people really talk, including slang and humor. My cousin, for example, spent six months in Canada, and her English improved more than in four years of classes at home. But I'd say a classroom gives you a good foundation in grammar first, so the best plan is to do both.
points: Supports the view with an example

stem: Some schools now start teaching a foreign language to children as young as five. Do you think this is a good idea?
explanation: Yes, I think it's a very good idea. Young children seem to pick up new sounds and words very naturally, and they're usually not afraid of making mistakes, which helps them speak more freely. If they start early, they also have many more years to practice before they finish school. My niece started English classes at five through songs and games, and now, at nine, her pronunciation is better than mine. However, the lessons should be fun and relaxed, not like a serious exam subject. If small children feel pressure, they might lose interest in the language completely.
points: Adds a condition about teaching style

stem: With translation technology improving so quickly, do you think people will still need to learn foreign languages in the future?
explanation: Yes, I think people will still need to learn languages, even with great translation apps. Translation tools are really useful for simple things, like reading a menu or asking for directions, and I use them myself when I travel. But they can't fully replace real understanding. When you speak someone's language, you can build a closer relationship, understand their jokes and learn about their culture. In business, too, people trust you more if you make the effort to speak their language. Also, learning a language trains your brain. So I think translation tools will help, but they won't replace learning.
points: Explains why learning is still valuable

title: Parks and green spaces
text: You have agreed to take part in a city survey about parks and green spaces. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: How often do you spend time in a park or other green space, and what do you do there?
explanation: I go to a park about twice a week, usually the one near my apartment. On weekday evenings I often walk there after classes, just for twenty or thirty minutes, to get some fresh air and relax after sitting all day. On Sundays I sometimes meet friends there for a picnic or a game of badminton. There's a small lake in the middle, and I like sitting on a bench by the water and reading. I find that even a short time in a green space helps me feel calmer, especially during busy exam periods when I'm stressed.
points: Answers how often in the first sentence
Uses present simple and frequency words

stem: Would you rather spend a free day in a city park or out in the countryside? Why?
explanation: I'd rather spend a free day out in the countryside. In a city park you can still hear traffic and see buildings all around you, and on weekends it's usually crowded. In the countryside, it's really quiet, the air is cleaner, and there's much more space to walk or explore. For example, last month a few friends and I took a train to a small village an hour away and hiked through the hills all day. I came back feeling completely refreshed. City parks are great for a quick break, but for a whole free day, the countryside is better.
points: Gives reasons such as quiet and space
Supports it with a specific trip
Briefly compares with the other option

stem: Some people think cities should use empty land for parks, while others think it should be used for new housing. What is your opinion?
explanation: That's a tough choice, but I'd say cities need to find a balance, and in many cases I'd choose parks. Parks improve people's physical and mental health, and they help cool cities down in summer. Once land is built on, it's almost impossible to turn it back into green space. In my old neighborhood, for example, an empty field became a park with a playground, and it completely changed the area. Families started spending time outside together. That said, housing is a real need, so maybe cities could build taller buildings in some places and save other land for parks.
points: Supports it with a local example
Recognizes the housing need and suggests a balance

stem: How do you think green spaces in cities might change in the next twenty years?
explanation: I think green spaces will become more creative and more spread out. Since land in cities is so expensive, we'll probably see more gardens on rooftops, plants growing on the walls of buildings and small parks built on old roads or railway lines. Some cities are already doing this. In my city, for example, an old bridge was turned into a long garden with walking paths, and it's always busy. I also think there'll be more community gardens where neighbors grow their own vegetables. So even if there isn't more land, cities will find new ways to be greener.
points: Explains why the change is likely

title: Friendship and staying in touch
text: You are participating in a study about friendship and how people stay in touch. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Tell me about a close friend and how you usually spend time together.
explanation: One of my closest friends is Mateo. We met in our first year of high school when we sat next to each other in science class, and we've been friends ever since. These days we're at different universities, so we don't see each other as often. When we're both home for the holidays, we usually go for long walks, play video games or try a new restaurant. During the semester, we send each other funny videos and talk on the phone about once a week. What I like most about him is that I can be completely honest with him.

stem: Do you prefer having a small group of close friends or a large group of friends? Why?
explanation: I prefer having a small group of close friends. With just a few people, I can really get to know them well, and I know I can count on them when I have a problem. With a large group, the relationships tend to stay on the surface, and it's hard to find time for everyone. For example, when I had a difficult time during my first semester, it was my three closest friends who called me every few days and helped me feel better. A big group is fun for parties, but for real support, a few good friends matter more.
points: Explains reasons such as trust and depth
Supports it with a personal example
Mentions a benefit of the other option

stem: Some people say social media helps people stay close to their friends. Others say it makes friendships weaker. What do you think?
explanation: I think social media does both, but overall it helps friendships if you use it well. It's great for staying in touch with people who live far away. I have friends in three different countries, and without messaging apps and photos, we'd probably have lost contact years ago. However, social media can also make friendships feel shallow. Clicking like on someone's photo isn't the same as having a real conversation. I've noticed that I sometimes think I know what's happening in a friend's life, but I haven't actually talked to them in months. So it's useful, but it can't replace real contact.
points: Explains a benefit with an example

stem: In the future, do you think people will have more friends or fewer friends? Why?
explanation: I think people will probably have more contacts, but fewer close friends. Technology makes it very easy to meet people online through games, study groups or hobby communities, so many people will have friends all over the world. But at the same time, people are moving cities more often for study and work, and they're busier than ever, so it's harder to keep deep friendships going. My parents, for example, still have friends from their childhood, but I've already moved three times and lost touch with some people. So I'd say the number will grow, but the closeness might not.
points: Explains the reasons for the change
Supports it with a personal comparison

title: Housing and roommates
text: You have agreed to take part in a study about student housing. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Can you describe where you live now and who you live with?
explanation: Right now I live in a two-bedroom apartment about fifteen minutes from campus by bus. I share it with one roommate, Priya, who's studying economics. We each have our own bedroom, and we share the kitchen, the bathroom and a small living room. It's not very big, but it's bright, and the rent is reasonable because we split it. We get along well. We usually cook dinner together a few times a week, and we've made a cleaning schedule so we don't argue about chores. The only problem is the neighbors upstairs, who are sometimes quite noisy at night.
points: Answers where and with whom directly
Explains how the living situation works
Mentions a positive and a problem

stem: Would you rather live alone or with roommates? Why?
explanation: I'd rather live with roommates, at least while I'm a student. The main reason is cost. Rent is very expensive near the university, and sharing it makes a huge difference. But it's not just about money. Living with other people also means I'm less lonely, especially since my family lives far away. For example, when I was sick last winter, my roommate went to the pharmacy for me and made soup. If I'd lived alone, it would've been a really hard week. Of course, you have to accept less privacy, but I think the advantages are bigger.
points: Gives reasons such as cost and company
Supports them with a personal example

stem: Some universities require first-year students to live in campus dormitories. Do you think this is a good policy?
explanation: I think it's a good policy for most students. In the first year, everything is new, and living in a dormitory makes it much easier to meet people and feel part of the university. You're close to classes, the library and the dining hall, so you don't waste time commuting. In my first year, for example, almost all my friends were people from my dorm floor, and we studied together for exams. However, universities should allow some exceptions, for instance for students who live with their families nearby or who can't afford the dormitory fees.

stem: How do you think student housing will change in the future?
explanation: I think student housing will become more shared and more flexible. Since cities are getting more expensive, I expect more buildings designed especially for students, with small private rooms and large shared kitchens, study areas and gyms. Some places near my campus already look like that. I also think more students will live with older people who have extra rooms, helping them with shopping in exchange for lower rent. I've read about programs like this, and they sound like a smart idea. And of course, technology will help, for example with apps that match compatible roommates before they move in.
points: Uses a current example as support

title: Watching and playing sports
text: You are taking part in a study about sports and entertainment. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Do you follow any sports? Tell me about the sports you watch or play.
explanation: Yes, I follow cricket and basketball. Cricket is really popular in my family, so I grew up watching big matches on TV with my father and my brothers. We still message each other during important games, even though I live far away now. I also play basketball, but just for fun. Every Wednesday evening, I join a pickup game at the university gym with some classmates. I'm not very tall, so I'm not a great player, but I enjoy the exercise and the friendly competition. It's also a nice way to forget about studying for a couple of hours.
points: Answers directly and names the sports
Describes watching and playing with details
Uses present and past tenses well

stem: Do you prefer watching sports at a stadium or at home? Why?
explanation: I prefer watching sports at a stadium, even though it's more expensive. The atmosphere is completely different. You're surrounded by thousands of fans who are cheering, singing and reacting to every play, and that energy is really exciting. At home it's comfortable, but it feels much calmer. For example, I once went to a big basketball game with friends, and when our team won in the last few seconds, the whole stadium jumped up at once. I'll never forget that moment. Of course, at home you get replays and a better view, so for everyday games I just watch on TV.
points: Supports it with a vivid example
Mentions an advantage of the other option

stem: Some people think professional athletes are paid too much money. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: I partly agree. Top athletes earn far more than doctors, nurses or teachers, who do work that's much more important for society, and that does seem unfair. On the other hand, athletes' salaries come from the huge amount of money that fans, TV companies and sponsors spend on sports. Their careers are also short, often ending in their early thirties, and they can get badly injured. A player I followed, for example, had to retire at twenty-six because of a knee injury. So I understand why they're paid so much, but I still think the gap is too large.

stem: How do you think technology will change the way people watch sports in the future?
explanation: I think technology will make watching sports much more interactive. Already, you can choose different camera angles on some streaming services and see live statistics about players. In the future, I expect people to use virtual reality headsets to feel like they're sitting in the stadium, even if they're at home in another country. A friend of mine tried a virtual reality basketball game recently, and he said it felt surprisingly real. I also think viewers will watch more short highlights on their phones rather than whole games, because people have less time and shorter attention spans.
points: Mentions a change in viewing habits

title: Teachers and mentors
text: You have agreed to take part in a study about the people who influence our learning. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Tell me about a teacher who had a big influence on you.
explanation: The teacher who influenced me most was my high school biology teacher, Ms. Amara. Before her class, I thought science was just memorizing facts, but she made it feel like solving mysteries. She often started a lesson with a question, like why leaves change color, and let us discuss it before explaining. She also took us on field trips to a nearby river to collect water samples. What I remember most is that she believed in me. When I got a bad grade, she stayed after class to help me. Because of her, I decided to study environmental science.
points: Identifies a specific teacher at once
Describes what made the teacher special

stem: Do you prefer teachers who are strict or teachers who are relaxed? Why?
explanation: I prefer teachers who are somewhere in the middle, but if I have to choose, I'd pick a strict teacher. When a teacher has clear rules and high expectations, I know exactly what I need to do, and I tend to work harder. Relaxed teachers are pleasant, but sometimes the class becomes noisy and people don't take it seriously. For example, my math teacher in high school was very strict about homework, and at first I didn't like it. But by the end of the year, my grades had improved a lot. Strict doesn't have to mean unkind, though.
points: Explains reasons such as clarity and effort
Supports it with a personal example

stem: Some people believe that having a mentor is more important for success than having a good education. What do you think?
explanation: I think both are important, but a mentor can make a bigger difference in some ways. A good education gives you knowledge, but a mentor shows you how to use it in the real world. They can give advice about decisions, introduce you to useful people and help you avoid mistakes. My older cousin, for instance, works in engineering, and his advice about which courses and internships to choose helped me more than any brochure. Still, a mentor can't replace the basic skills you learn at school. So I'd say education is the foundation, and a mentor helps you build on it.
points: Supports the view with an example

stem: In the future, do you think artificial intelligence could take over some of the work that teachers do? Why or why not?
explanation: I think artificial intelligence will take over some parts of teaching, but not the most important parts. AI tools are already good at things like checking simple exercises, explaining grammar rules or giving extra practice, and they can do it for each student at their own level. I use an app like that for vocabulary, and it really helps. But a teacher does much more than give information. A good teacher notices when a student is confused or upset, motivates the class and helps students get along with each other. So I'd say AI will be a helpful assistant, not a replacement.
points: Explains what AI can do well
Explains what teachers do that AI cannot

title: Photography and memories
text: You are taking part in a study about photography and how people keep their memories. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: How often do you take photos, and what do you usually take pictures of?
explanation: I take photos almost every day, but mostly with my phone. A lot of them are just practical, like pictures of the whiteboard after class or a timetable at the bus stop. But I also love taking pictures of food and of the sky. Where I live now, the sunsets are amazing, so I often stop on my way home to take a picture. When I travel or see my family, I take many more photos, especially of people. My phone has more than five thousand pictures on it right now, which is a bit too many, honestly.
points: Answers how often in the first sentence
Adds details and a personal touch

stem: Do you prefer keeping photos on your phone or printing them out? Why?
explanation: Mostly I keep photos on my phone, because it's so easy. I can find any picture in seconds, share it with friends right away, and I don't need any space to store them. But I do print a few special ones. For example, last year I printed photos from my sister's wedding and put them in an album for my grandmother, and she looks at it all the time. I think printed photos feel more meaningful because you choose them carefully. So for everyday pictures, my phone is better, but for important memories, I prefer prints.
points: Gives an example of the other option

stem: Some people think that taking so many photos stops us from enjoying the moment. Do you agree?
explanation: Yes, I agree to some extent. When people are busy taking pictures, they're looking at a screen instead of experiencing what's around them. At concerts, for example, you often see hundreds of people holding up their phones and recording the whole show. I did that once at a festival, and later I realized I barely remembered the performance itself. On the other hand, photos help us remember things we might forget. So I think the best approach is to take a few photos quickly, then put the phone away and really enjoy the moment. That's what I try to do now.
points: Supports the view with a personal example

stem: How do you think the way people record and share their memories will change in the future?
explanation: I think people will record memories in much richer ways. Instead of just photos and videos, we might record 3D scenes that we can walk through later with virtual reality glasses. Some phones can already make simple 3D scans. I also expect that apps will organize our memories automatically, for example making a short video of your year with music. My phone already does this, and it's actually quite emotional to watch. The challenge will be privacy and storage, because people will create huge amounts of data. Some people might even start choosing to record less.

title: Working from home
text: You have agreed to take part in a research study about working and studying from home. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Have you ever worked or studied from home for a long period? What was it like?
explanation: Yes, I studied from home for almost a whole semester when my university moved classes online for a while. At first it was nice. I didn't have to commute, and I could wear comfortable clothes and sleep a little later. But after a few weeks it became harder. My desk was in my bedroom, so it was difficult to separate study time from free time, and I often worked late into the night. I also missed seeing my classmates. What helped was making a fixed schedule and taking a walk every afternoon. Still, I was happy to return to campus.
points: Answers yes or no with context

stem: Would you rather work from home or in an office? Why?
explanation: I'd rather work in an office, at least for most of the week. The main reason is that I need a clear line between work and home. In an office, I'm focused while I'm there, and when I leave, I can really relax. At home, I'd probably keep checking emails all evening. I also think you learn a lot from colleagues just by being around them. During my internship, for example, I picked up useful tips simply by listening to the people at the desks next to me. That said, one or two days at home each week would be nice.
points: Gives reasons about focus and learning
Supports with an example from experience

stem: Some people say working from home is better for the environment. Do you agree? Why or why not?
explanation: Yes, I mostly agree. When people work from home, they don't drive or take buses to an office every day, so there's less traffic and less air pollution. Companies can also use smaller offices, which need less heating, cooling and electricity. In my city, for example, the roads were noticeably quieter on Fridays once many companies allowed home working that day. However, it's not completely simple. People at home use their own heating and computers all day, so some of the energy use just moves to houses. But overall, I think the benefit from less commuting is bigger.

stem: Do you think working from home will become the normal way of working in the future?
explanation: I don't think it'll become the normal way for everyone, but I think a mix will become normal. Many jobs, like nursing, cooking or building, simply can't be done from home. For office jobs, though, I expect most people to split their time, maybe working at home two or three days a week and going to the office for meetings and teamwork. That's already what my mother's company does, and her colleagues seem to like it. Cities might change too, with fewer big office buildings downtown and more small shared workspaces in neighborhoods. So the future will probably be flexible.
points: Explains why it differs by job
Mentions a broader effect on cities

title: Time management
text: You are participating in a university study about how students manage their time. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: How do you usually plan your week when you have a lot of things to do?
explanation: When I have a busy week, I usually plan everything on Sunday evening. I open the calendar on my phone and write down all my classes, deadlines and work shifts first. Then I find the free blocks of time and decide which assignment I'll do in each one. I also make a short to-do list every morning with the three most important tasks for that day. For example, last week I had two essays and a presentation, and planning like this helped me finish everything a day early. It doesn't always work perfectly, but it really reduces my stress.
points: Answers directly with a clear method

stem: Do you prefer to finish tasks early or to work close to the deadline? Why?
explanation: I prefer to finish tasks early, although I don't always manage it. When I finish early, I have time to check my work and fix mistakes, and I don't have to worry about it for days. Working close to the deadline makes me nervous, and I usually make silly errors because I'm rushing. For example, last year I wrote a lab report the night before it was due, and I forgot to include a whole section of results. I lost a lot of points for that. Since then, I try to finish everything at least two days before the deadline.
points: Gives reasons such as quality and stress
Supports it with a personal example

stem: Some people think universities should teach time management as a required course. What is your opinion?
