explanation: I think it's a good idea, but it shouldn't be a long course. Many first-year students struggle because, for the first time, nobody is telling them when to study. They have more free time, but also bigger assignments, and some fall behind quickly. A short required workshop in the first few weeks could teach useful skills like planning, setting priorities and avoiding distractions. At my university, there was an optional workshop like that, and the students who went told me it really helped. Making it required would reach the students who need it most but probably wouldn't sign up.
points: Explains why students need the skill

stem: Do you think people will have more free time or less free time in the future? Why?
explanation: I think it could go either way, but I'd guess people will have a little more free time. Technology is taking over many boring tasks, like cleaning with robot vacuums or paying bills automatically, and that saves time every week. Some companies are also testing a four-day working week. A company in my city tried it, and the workers said they were just as productive. On the other hand, phones make it easy for work to follow us home. So people may have more free hours, but they'll need to protect that time from work messages and screens.
points: Explains reasons linked to technology and work

title: Public art in cities
text: You have agreed to take part in a city council survey about public art. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Is there any public art, like a statue or a mural, that you see regularly? Tell me about it.
explanation: Yes, there's a huge mural on the side of a building near my bus stop that I see every day. It shows a group of children flying kites over the river, with really bright colors like orange, blue and yellow. It was painted a few years ago by local artists, and I've heard that some students from a nearby school helped design it. Before the mural, that wall was gray and covered in old posters, so it really changed the street. Whenever I'm waiting for the bus on a bad day, looking at it somehow cheers me up.
points: Answers directly with a specific artwork

stem: Do you prefer traditional public art, like statues, or modern art, like murals and installations? Why?
explanation: I prefer modern public art like murals and installations. They usually feel more connected to the people who live in a place today, and they often involve the community in creating them. They're also more colorful and surprising, so they make ordinary streets more interesting. For example, last summer my city put large colorful benches shaped like animals in the main square, and children loved climbing on them. Traditional statues can be impressive and important for history, but many of them are of people I don't know much about, so I tend to walk past them without noticing.
points: Gives reasons such as connection and color
Supports it with a specific example
Comments briefly on the other type

stem: Some people think city governments should spend money on public art, while others think the money should go to things like roads and hospitals. What do you think?
explanation: I think cities should spend some money on public art, but only a small part of their budget. Roads and hospitals are basic needs, so they should always come first. However, public art doesn't usually cost very much compared to those things, and it can make a real difference. It makes neighborhoods more attractive, gives people a sense of pride and can even bring tourists and customers to local businesses. In my city, for instance, a street full of murals became a popular place for visitors, and new cafés opened there. So a small investment can bring real benefits.
points: Explains why basic needs come first
Explains the benefits of public art

stem: How do you think public art might change in the future?
explanation: I think public art will become more digital and more interactive. We already see art made with light, like colored images projected onto buildings at night, and I expect much more of that because it's easy to change. There might also be art that reacts to people, for example a wall that changes colors when you walk past or plays sounds when you touch it. Last winter my city had a light festival like this, and the streets were packed every evening. Some public art might even exist only in augmented reality, visible through your phone camera. It'll be exciting to see.
points: Supports it with a current example

title: Pets and animals
text: You are taking part in a study about pets and people's relationships with animals. You will answer an interviewer's questions.

stem: Do you have, or have you ever had, a pet? Tell me about it.
explanation: Yes, when I was growing up, my family had a cat named Pepper. She was gray with white paws, and she came to us as a tiny kitten that my sister found near our school. Pepper was quite independent. She spent most of the day sleeping in the sun by the window, but every evening she would sit next to me while I did my homework. I think she liked the warm lamp more than me, though. She lived with us for fourteen years. I don't have a pet now because my apartment doesn't allow them, but I really miss having one.
points: Answers yes or no with a specific pet
Uses past tenses and 'would' for habits

stem: Which do you think make better pets, cats or dogs? Why?
explanation: I think cats make better pets, especially for people who live in cities. Cats are independent, so they're fine on their own while you're at work or at school all day. They don't need to be walked, and they're usually happy in a small apartment. Dogs are wonderful and very loyal, but they need a lot of time, exercise and attention. For example, my neighbor has a big dog, and she has to come home at lunch every day to take it outside. That would be impossible with my schedule. So for a busy lifestyle, a cat is a better choice.
points: Recognizes a strength of the other option

stem: Some people believe that having a pet is good for children because it teaches them responsibility. Do you agree?
explanation: Yes, I agree. When children have a pet, they learn that another living thing depends on them. They have to remember to feed it, give it water and clean up after it, even when they don't feel like it. That's a great lesson in responsibility. Pets can also teach kindness and patience. When I was a child, I was in charge of feeding our cat every morning, and if I forgot, my parents made sure I understood why it mattered. However, parents still need to help, because young children can't do everything alone, and the animal's health comes first.
points: Supports it with a personal example

stem: Do you think more people will own pets in the future, or fewer? Why?
explanation: I think more people will own pets in the future, but smaller ones. Many people today live alone or in small apartments, and a pet gives them company and helps them feel less lonely. I've noticed that many of my friends have adopted cats or small dogs in the last few years. Also, more people work from home now, so they have time to care for an animal. However, housing could be a problem, since many buildings don't allow pets, and caring for an animal is getting more expensive. So the number will grow, but people will choose easier pets.
